title: Strict-local invariant connected pieces detect ampleness over a Dedekind base
statement: Let $D$ be a Noetherian integrally closed domain of Krull dimension at most one, put $S=\operatorname{Spec}D$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum], and put $K=\operatorname{Frac}D$. Let $H\to S$ be a smooth separated group scheme of finite type with geometrically connected fibres [def-pc-scheme, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-finite-type-morphism, def-weil-connected-scheme]. A group scheme has multiplication, inverse and identity satisfying the group identities (the relative version of [def-sc-group-scheme]); separated means its diagonal is a closed immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Let $X\to S$ be smooth, separated and of finite type, with an action $a:H\times_SX\to X$ satisfying unit and associativity [def-pc-fibre-product], and let $L$ be an invertible $\mathcal O_X$-module [def-sc-invertible-module]. Consider all flat morphisms $T=\operatorname{Spec}R\to S$ [def-weil-flat-morphism] for which either $R$ is a separably closed field [def-pc-separably-closed], or $R$ is a strictly henselian discrete valuation ring [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring]. Here strictly henselian means that the residue field is separably closed and every simple residue root of a monic polynomial lifts to a root in $R$. For such $T$, consider every nonempty connected open and closed subscheme $Y\subseteq X_T$ [def-weil-open-immersion] such that $Y\to T$ is surjective, $Y$ is invariant under $H_T$, and its generic fibre is geometrically connected. Invariant means the restricted action $H_T\times_TY\to X_T$ factors through $Y$; geometrically connected means connected after every extension of the fraction field of $R$ [def-pc-geometrically-irreducible]. Write $L_Y$ for the tensor pullback of $L$ to $Y$ [def-pc-module-pullback]. If $L_Y$ is ample [def-weil-pbc-ample-invertible-module] for every one of these tests, then $L$ is ample on $X$. The empty $X$ is allowed.

proof.text: If $X$ is empty, it is quasi-compact and the pointwise ampleness condition is vacuous, so the conclusion follows. Henceforth fix a prime $\mathfrak p$ of $D$, and put $A=D_{\mathfrak p}$. The morphism $\operatorname{Spec}A\to S$ is flat by localization flatness and the affine flatness criterion. If $\mathfrak p=0$, then $A=K$ is a field. If $\mathfrak p\ne0$, the chain $0\subsetneq\mathfrak p$ and the dimension bound show that $D$ has dimension one and $\mathfrak p$ is maximal; the Dedekind localization theorem makes $A$ a DVR. We will prove ampleness after this localization and then descend it to a neighbourhood of $\mathfrak p$.

source.place: 6.4 Proposition 2, proof, printed pp.153–154 (PDF pp.159–160), initial local and component reductions; primary online scan read, local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Choose a faithfully flat affine extension $\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ as follows. For $A=K$, take a separable closure $B=K^{\mathrm{sep}}$; the field-extension fpqc theorem applies. For a DVR $A$, choose a geometric point $\bar x$ of $\operatorname{Spec}A$ over its closed point and take $B=\mathcal O^{\mathrm{sh}}_{\operatorname{Spec}A,\bar x}$. The strict-henselization local-structure theorem says $B$ is local and strictly henselian, i.e. henselian with separably closed residue field; the strict-henselization DVR theorem, for this same ring, says $A\to B$ is flat local and $B$ is a DVR. The henselian root-lifting equivalence turns the idempotent-lifting form of henselian into the lifting of simple residue roots of monic polynomials, so $B$ is strictly henselian in the sense of the statement. A flat local map is faithfully flat and therefore surjective on spectra. Since both spectra are affine, this is a one-member fpqc cover: over any affine open of the target its inverse image is affine and maps onto that open. Composition of flat morphisms makes $T=\operatorname{Spec}B\to S$ flat, so $T$ is among the tests in the hypothesis. Write $Z=X_T$, $G=H_T$, and $M=L|_Z$. Base change preserves smoothness, separatedness and finite type, and tensor pullback preserves invertibility.

source.place: 6.4 Proposition 2, proof, printed pp.153–154 (PDF pp.159–160), initial local and component reductions; primary online scan read, local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: The scheme $T$ is Noetherian and normal. For a field this is immediate. For a DVR its ideals are principal, hence finitely generated; its dimension is one and its maximal ideal has one generator, so the regular-local/normal equivalence makes $B$ integrally closed. The local rings of its spectrum are $B$ and its fraction field, hence normal. The finite-type Noetherian theorem makes $Z$ Noetherian, and smooth ascent makes $Z$ normal. The normal-component theorem now gives finitely many pairwise disjoint clopen integral normal subschemes $C_i$ covering $Z$. They are exactly its nonempty connected components. Each is smooth and finite type over $T$ (restriction to a clopen in a Noetherian scheme); smoothness gives flatness and local finite presentation, so its structural map is open. For a trait, its nonempty image is therefore either all of $T$ or just its generic point. In the latter case, writing $\pi$ for a uniformizer, $C_i$ is entirely contained in $Z_{B[1/\pi]}$ and is a smooth separated finite-type scheme over $F=\operatorname{Frac}B$.

source.place: 6.4 Proposition 2, proof, printed pp.153–154 (PDF pp.159–160), initial local and component reductions; primary online scan read, local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Every $C_i$ is $G$-invariant. Indeed, for $z\in C_i$ with image $t\in T$, restrict the action to $G_{\kappa(z)}\to Z$. Its source is connected because the fibres of $H$ are geometrically connected and $\kappa(z)$ extends $\kappa(t)$. The image is connected and contains $z$ by the unit identity. It therefore lies in the connected component $C_i$. Every point of $G\times_TC_i$ lies over some such $z$, so the whole restricted action has image in $C_i$. By the definition of open subscheme, a morphism whose point image lies in this open factors uniquely through it. The identical argument applies to the clopen connected components after any field base change. Geometric connectedness of the fibres persists under base change simply because the defining quantifier already allows every field extension.

source.place: 6.4 Proposition 2, proof, printed pp.153–154 (PDF pp.159–160), initial local and component reductions; primary online scan read, local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: First consider any separably closed field $B$ with a flat map $T\to S$, not just the field chosen in step 2. For the decomposition of $Z=X_T$ from step 3, each $C_i$ is a nonempty smooth $B$-scheme. The density of separable closed points supplies a closed point with finite separable residue extension of $B$, which equals $B$ since $B$ is separably closed. Thus $C_i$ has a $B$-rational point. Since $C_i$ is connected, the connected-rational-point theorem makes it geometrically connected. It is surjective over $T$, and invariant by step 4, so the testing hypothesis gives $M|_{C_i}$ ample. Apply the finite-coproduct ampleness theorem with $Y_i=C_i$ and the isolated-point index set empty: $M$ is ample on $Z$. This includes $Z=\varnothing$, with both index sets empty.

source.place: 6.4 Proposition 2, proof, printed pp.153–154 (PDF pp.159–160), initial local and component reductions; primary online scan read, local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Now let $B$ be the strict henselian DVR of step 2 and take a component $C_i$ meeting the closed fibre. By step 3 it is smooth, finite type and surjective over $T$. The strict-local section-existence theorem supplies a section $T\to C_i$; only its assertion $C_i(T)\ne\varnothing$ is used. Its generic restriction is an $F$-rational point of $(C_i)_F$. Moreover $(C_i)_F=C_i\cap Z_{B[1/\pi]}$ is a nonempty open subscheme of the integral $C_i$, hence is integral and connected: every two of its nonempty opens are nonempty opens of an irreducible space and intersect. The connected-rational-point theorem therefore makes $(C_i)_F$ geometrically connected. Together with step 4 this verifies every hypothesis on a test $Y=C_i$ over $T$; the assumed test ampleness gives $M|_{C_i}$ ample.

source.place: 6.4 Proposition 2, proof, printed pp.153–154 (PDF pp.159–160), initial local and component reductions; primary online scan read, local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: For a component $C_i$ missing the closed fibre, regard it as a clopen subscheme of $Z_F$ as in step 3. Choose a separable closure $\Omega/F$. The composite $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to\operatorname{Spec}F\to T\to S$ is flat: the field-extension theorem, localization flatness, the affine criterion and composition prove this. Step 5, which was proved for every flat separably closed field test, makes $L|_{X_\Omega}$ ample. The inclusion $(C_i)_\Omega\to X_\Omega$ is clopen and therefore affine by the closed-embedding theorem. Affine pullback of an ample module gives ampleness on $(C_i)_\Omega$. Descend along the one-member fpqc field cover $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to\operatorname{Spec}F$, using the relative-ampleness descent theorem, to obtain ampleness on $C_i$. Here, and below, apply this spaces theorem to schemes via the Zariski/etale quasi-coherent equivalence: it identifies line modules, tensor pullbacks and their comparisons. For an affine target, the definition in that theorem identifies relative ampleness with absolute ampleness: the whole target is one of its affine opens, and conversely inverse images of other affine opens are affine pullbacks, so preserve ampleness.

source.place: 6.4 Proposition 2, proof, printed pp.153–154 (PDF pp.159–160), initial local and component reductions; primary online scan read, local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Steps 6 and 7 prove ampleness on every $C_i$ for the strict henselian DVR case. The finite-coproduct ampleness theorem, with no isolated-point summands, proves $M$ ample on all of $Z$. Together with step 5, this proves ampleness after the fpqc affine extension $\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ in both cases of step 2. Relative-ampleness fpqc descent, with the scheme/site identification and affine-target argument of step 7, gives $L_A$ ample on $X_A$. This holds for every prime $\mathfrak p$ of $D$.

source.place: 6.4 Proposition 2, proof, printed pp.153–154 (PDF pp.159–160), initial local and component reductions; primary online scan read, local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: For the fixed $\mathfrak p$, write $D_{\mathfrak p}=\varinjlim_{f\notin\mathfrak p}D_f$, indexed by divisibility, with initial object $f=1$. The localization-colimit and spectrum-limit theorems identify $\operatorname{Spec}D_{\mathfrak p}$ with the inverse limit of these principal opens. The fibre-product limit theorem then identifies $X_A$ with the inverse limit of $X_{D_f}$. All transition maps are affine: those between the bases are maps of affine schemes, and the source transitions are their base changes. Each $X_{D_f}$ is Noetherian, since its base is Noetherian and its structural map is finite type; it is also separated, hence quasi-separated. Thus the qcqs hypotheses of ample affine-limit descent hold. By step 8 the limit pullback $L_A$ is ample, so that theorem gives some $f\notin\mathfrak p$ for which $L|_{X_{D_f}}$ is ample. This is a neighbourhood of the base point, rather than just a fibrewise assertion.

source.place: Tag 09MT, lemma-limit-ample; applied to the principal-neighbourhood limit in the first paragraph of BLR 6.4 Proposition 2.

proof.text: The principal neighbourhoods supplied by step 9 for all primes cover $S$. Choose finitely many, since $S$ is affine and quasi-compact. They form an fpqc cover: their inclusions are flat localization maps, and on any affine open $V$ their intersections with $V$ are quasi-compact opens of the Noetherian scheme $S$, hence have finite affine covers whose images cover $V$. On each covering member, $L$ is absolutely and hence relatively ample by the affine-target argument of step 7. Relative-ampleness fpqc descent gives $L$ relatively ample over $S$; since $S$ itself is affine, its defining condition applied to the whole $S$ says exactly that $L$ is ample on $X$.
